title: AI Unlocked: Law & Legal Practice
blurb: For lawyers, paralegals, and compliance teams: research and drafting acceleration, contract review workflows, the legal-AI tool market compared, and the professional-responsibility rules (competence, confidentiality, candor) that make or break adoption.

modules.d: What AI changes in legal work, the duties that do not change, and the cautionary cases every lawyer must know.
modules.body:
Law is a language profession — and AI is a language technology

Much legal work is reading, analysing and producing text: research memos, contracts, pleadings, opinions, correspondence. Generative AI therefore touches the core of legal practice more directly than most professions. Used well, it compresses hours of first-draft work and document review into minutes. Used carelessly, it produces confident, polished, entirely fictional law.

The cautionary case

In Mata v. Avianca (U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York, 2023), lawyers filed a brief citing judicial decisions that did not exist — generated by ChatGPT. When questioned, they did not promptly correct the record. The court imposed sanctions, finding they had abandoned their responsibilities. Since then, courts in many jurisdictions have reported similar incidents of fabricated citations and misquoted authorities, with sanctions, costs orders and disciplinary referrals. The lesson is not "never use AI"; it is every authority must be verified in an authoritative source by a lawyer before it is relied on.

Specialised tools are not immune. A 2024 Stanford study of leading AI legal research tools from major legal publishers found that even systems grounded in legal databases produced incorrect or misgrounded answers in a meaningful share of test queries. Better tools reduce the risk; they do not remove the duty to verify.

Professional duties that do not change

Codes of professional conduct differ across jurisdictions, but core duties are remarkably consistent:

  • Competence — including understanding the benefits and risks of the technology you use. The American Bar Association's Model Rules (comment 8 to Rule 1.1) explicitly include technological competence, and ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024) applies the Model Rules to generative AI.
  • Confidentiality — protecting client information, including from tools that store or train on inputs.
  • Candour to the tribunal — never presenting false statements of law or fact; correcting errors promptly.
  • Supervision — responsibility for the work of juniors, staff and the tools they use.
  • Communication — keeping clients informed, including about significant use of AI where relevant.
  • Reasonable fees — billing that reflects the work actually done.
  • Independence and judgement — the lawyer, not the tool, provides legal advice.

Practising in a mixed legal system

Many African jurisdictions combine legal traditions, and AI tools trained mainly on US and UK material handle them poorly. Cameroon is bijural: common-law traditions apply in the North-West and South-West regions and civil-law traditions elsewhere, with statutes in English and French, alongside customary law. Business law is largely harmonised through the OHADA Uniform Acts, interpreted by national courts and the Common Court of Justice and Arbitration (CCJA) in Abidjan. An AI tool may confidently apply English common law or French civil law to a question governed by an OHADA Uniform Act or Cameroonian statute. Jurisdiction-specific verification is therefore essential.

Where AI adds value in legal work

  • Summarising long documents, judgments, transcripts and contracts.
  • First drafts of standard documents, letters and clauses from approved templates.
  • Issue spotting and structuring research questions.
  • Comparing documents and identifying deviations from a standard.
  • Translation between English and French — with legal review of terms of art.
  • Plain-language explanations for clients.
  • Large-scale document review in disputes and due diligence, with appropriate validation.

The changing shape of legal work

As routine drafting and review accelerate, value shifts toward judgement, strategy, negotiation, advocacy, client relationships and verification. Junior lawyers still need to learn the fundamentals — otherwise they cannot evaluate AI output. Firms and legal departments must redesign training so juniors learn with AI without skipping the skills that make them competent.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal practice AI advisor. Ask me about my jurisdiction(s), practice area, firm or department size and current tools. Identify five use cases where AI could save the most time with manageable risk, and for each specify the verification step and confidentiality safeguard required. Then list the professional-conduct duties in my jurisdiction that I should check apply to AI use, noting that I must verify them against the official rules.

📚 Glossary

  • Fabricated citation: an AI-generated reference to a case or authority that does not exist
  • Technological competence: understanding the benefits and risks of the technology a lawyer uses
  • Candour to the tribunal: duty not to mislead the court on law or fact
  • Bijural system: a legal system combining two legal traditions
  • OHADA: Organisation for the Harmonisation of Business Law in Africa

📖 References

  • Mata v. Avianca, Inc., No. 22-cv-1461 (S.D.N.Y. 2023) — sanctions order.
  • American Bar Association — Model Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.1 cmt. 8; Formal Opinion 512 (2024) on generative AI tools.
  • Magesh, V. et al. (2024). Hallucination-free? Assessing the reliability of leading AI legal research tools. Stanford RegLab/HAI.
  • OHADA — Treaty and Uniform Acts; Common Court of Justice and Arbitration (CCJA).

quiz.q: An associate in New York files a brief with three AI-suggested case citations. Opposing counsel says two cannot be found. Following the lessons of Mata v. Avianca, what should the associate do first?
opts: File a short letter withdrawing the whole brief and request a fresh deadline from the judge
Wait for the court to raise the issue, then explain that the AI tool generated the citations
Promptly check the cases in an authoritative database and correct the record with the court
Ask the AI tool to supply the full text of the two cases so they can be attached to a reply
quiz.x: In Mata the sanctions turned partly on failing to promptly correct the record; candour requires verifying and correcting quickly. Withdrawing the brief is a runner-up but skips verification and may be unnecessary if one citation is valid.

quiz.q: A Douala law firm is choosing between a general AI assistant and a publisher's legal research AI that is grounded in its databases. A partner says the grounded tool removes the need to check citations. What is the best response?
opts: Agree for common-law questions, but keep checking civil-law and OHADA citations
Agree, provided the tool shows a link next to each authority that it cites
Disagree, because grounded tools are generally less accurate than general assistants
Disagree: studies found grounded tools still erred, so verification remains required
quiz.x: The 2024 Stanford study found grounded legal tools still produced incorrect or misgrounded answers in a meaningful share of queries. Links speed verification; they do not replace it. Grounded tools are usually more reliable, not less.

quiz.q: A Bamenda lawyer asks an AI chatbot about the formation requirements for a company limited by shares. The answer cites the UK Companies Act 2006. What is the most likely problem?
opts: The matter is governed by the OHADA Uniform Act, which the tool may have missed
The tool should have cited French company law, as Cameroon's civil code governs
Common-law rules apply in Bamenda, so the UK Act is binding persuasive authority here
The UK Act was amended recently, so the cited sections may be outdated
quiz.x: Company law in Cameroon is largely harmonised under the OHADA Uniform Acts, across both common-law and civil-law regions. AI tools trained on US and UK material often misapply foreign law; the common-law region does not make UK statutes govern.

quiz.q: A US state bar member asks whether technological competence is part of a lawyer's duty. Which source from the module most directly supports this for jurisdictions following the ABA Model Rules?
opts: Model Rule 1.6 on confidentiality, which bars any use of cloud-based software tools
Comment 8 to Model Rule 1.1, which covers the benefits and risks of relevant technology
ABA Formal Opinion 512, which requires bar-certified AI tools for client work
Model Rule 3.3 on candour, which defines the technical skills a lawyer must hold
quiz.x: Comment 8 to Rule 1.1 explicitly includes technological competence; Opinion 512 (2024) applies the Model Rules to generative AI but does not create a certification scheme. State adoption varies, so lawyers should check their own rules.

quiz.q: A senior partner in Yaounde wants first-year associates to use AI for all research memos from day one. What is the module's main concern?
opts: Juniors who skip the fundamentals may not be able to evaluate AI output
Associates would bill fewer hours, reducing the firm's revenue from junior work
Clients may object to paying associates' rates for AI-produced memoranda
The firm's AI licence may not cover users who are not yet fully admitted
quiz.x: The module stresses that juniors still need fundamentals, otherwise they cannot evaluate AI output; training must be redesigned, not abandoned. Fee concerns are real but secondary to competence.

quiz.q: A company in Garoua has a sales dispute with a supplier from Côte d'Ivoire. An AI tool answers by applying the French Civil Code to the contract. What should the lawyer check first?
opts: Whether the French Civil Code was updated after the tool's training cutoff
Whether the contract can be treated as consumer sale under Cameroonian law
Whether the Ivorian supplier would accept French law as a neutral choice
Whether an OHADA Uniform Act, such as on general commercial law, governs
quiz.x: Commercial sales between businesses in OHADA states are largely governed by the Uniform Act on General Commercial Law. AI tools may confidently apply French law to OHADA questions; jurisdiction-specific verification comes first.

quiz.q: A legal department in Johannesburg wants to know which task offers the best time saving with manageable risk. Which fits the module best?
opts: Answering client questions on new legislation directly from an AI chatbot
Summarising long judgments and contracts, with a lawyer reviewing the summary
Drafting court submissions from scratch, with authorities to be checked by a junior later
Advising on the likely outcome of a dispute using AI's estimate of odds
quiz.x: Summarising long documents with review is listed as a high-value use. Drafting submissions is possible, but litigation drafting carries the highest risk and 'check later' invites error.

quiz.q: A client in Buea asks whether its lawyer used AI on its matter and whether that affects the bill. Under the core duties in the module, which pair is most directly engaged?
opts: Supervision and competence
Confidentiality and candour
Communication and reasonable fees
Candour and lawyer independence
quiz.x: Keeping clients informed about significant AI use and billing for work actually done are the duties of communication and reasonable fees. Confidentiality may also arise, but the question is about disclosure and billing.

quiz.q: A US litigator finds, after filing, that one quotation in her brief, generated with AI help, does not appear in the cited case. The case itself is real. What does candour require?
opts: Correct it quietly in the reply brief without drawing attention to it
Nothing, because the case exists and the paraphrase is close enough
Ask opposing counsel whether they object before taking any action
Promptly notify the court and correct the misquotation in a filing
quiz.x: Candour to the tribunal requires correcting false statements of law promptly; a fabricated quotation is a false statement even if the case exists. A quiet fix in the reply is the runner-up but is not a clear correction.

quiz.q: Cameroon's business law is interpreted by national courts and a regional court. A trainee asks which court sits at the apex for OHADA Uniform Act questions. What is the best answer?
opts: The Common Court of Justice and Arbitration in Abidjan
The CEMAC Court of Justice, sitting in N'Djamena, Chad
The Supreme Court of Cameroon, sitting in Yaounde
The ECOWAS Court of Justice, sitting in Abuja
quiz.x: The CCJA in Abidjan interprets OHADA Uniform Acts and hears cassation appeals on them. The national Supreme Court is the runner-up but its role on Uniform Act questions is limited; check current procedure for each matter.

facts.t: Sanction imposed in Mata v. Avianca for filing ChatGPT-fabricated case citations.
facts.more: S.D.N.Y., 2023. The court stressed that the lawyers failed to correct the record promptly. Using AI wasn't the failure. Abandoning verification and candour was.

facts.t: ABA Formal Opinion on lawyers' use of generative AI tools (2024).
facts.more: It applies the existing Model Rules (competence, confidentiality, communication, candour, supervision, fees) to generative AI. It is persuasive outside the US, but check your own bar's rules.

facts.t: OHADA member states, mostly in West and Central Africa, including Cameroon.
facts.more: Uniform Acts harmonise business law across them, and the CCJA in Abidjan is the common supreme court for their interpretation. Tools trained on US/UK law often miss this layer.

facts.t: Cameroon combines common law (North-West, South-West) and civil law elsewhere, plus customary law.
facts.more: Statutes exist in English and French. An AI answer that applies English or French law to an OHADA question is a typical, confident error.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the urgent brief
plaibox.intro: You are an associate in Yaoundé. A filing deadline is tomorrow. Scoring: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: A general AI assistant gives you four CCJA decisions supporting your argument.
o: Cite them all, adding 'as reported' after each to be safe
Hedging doesn't cure a fabricated citation. You'd be misleading the court.
Find each decision in an authoritative source and read it
Every authority must be verified by a lawyer before reliance.
Cite only the two that sound most familiar from practice
Familiarity is not verification. Either could be invented.

steps.s: Two decisions don't exist. The other two are real but one says the opposite.
o: Drop all four cases and argue purely from first principles
Safe, but the one real supporting decision is useful once verified.
Rely on the one verified decision and keep researching
Use only what you've read and confirmed. Keep researching for more.
Keep the contrary case but quote only its helpful sentence
Selective quotation that misstates a holding breaches candour.

steps.s: After filing, you discover a pinpoint reference is wrong.
o: Notify the court promptly and correct it
Prompt correction is the candour duty. Mata turned on its absence.
Wait and fix it in the reply brief
You do correct it, but the delay is a risk if the error matters.
Leave it; the opponent may not notice
Knowingly leaving an error on the record breaches candour.

steps.s: Your partner asks how this happened and what changes.
o: Ban all AI tools across the firm, effective immediately
Understandable, but it forfeits real gains. Controls work better.
Add a verification checklist and training for AI-aided filings
Visible verification and supervision are the durable fix.
Tell the court it was the AI tool's fault, not the firm's
'The AI did it' is not a defence. Lawyers stay responsible.

plaibox.win: Model conduct: verify, rely only on what you've read, correct promptly, fix the system.
plaibox.lose: Review Mata v. Avianca and the core duties. Verification and candour are non-negotiable.

modules.d: Structured, verifiable workflows for legal research, analysis and drafting.
modules.body:
Research: AI as accelerator, not authority

A disciplined AI-assisted research workflow keeps authoritative sources at the centre. Step 1 — Frame the question: identify the jurisdiction, governing law, facts, procedural posture and the precise legal question. AI can help break a complex problem into sub-issues and suggest search terms in English and French. Step 2 — Find the law in authoritative sources: official gazettes, codes, OHADA Uniform Acts, court reporters, recognised databases. AI-integrated research platforms can speed this, but the source documents are what count. Step 3 — Read and analyse the actual texts. AI can summarise long judgments and extract holdings, but you must read the relevant passages yourself. Step 4 — Synthesise the rule and its application. Step 5 — Verify every citation, quotation, pinpoint reference and the current status of the law (amended, repealed, overruled, appealed).

Quotation discipline. AI tools frequently "quote" language that does not appear in the source, or blend paraphrase and quotation. Never put text in quotation marks unless you have copied it from the authoritative source yourself and checked the page or paragraph reference.

Structuring analysis: IRAC and its variants

Legal analysis is commonly structured as Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion (IRAC), or CREAC (Conclusion, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion) for persuasive writing. In civil-law traditions, the syllogisme juridique — major premise (rule), minor premise (facts), conclusion — serves the same purpose. AI is helpful for testing structure: ask it to identify which element is weak, which counter-arguments are unaddressed, and which facts are missing.

Drafting with templates and playbooks

The most reliable drafting workflows begin from approved precedents — the firm's or department's templates and clause library — rather than AI generating documents from nothing. Provide AI with the template, the deal terms or facts, and specific instructions; ask it to adapt clauses, flag deviations and draft explanatory notes. This keeps drafts consistent with house standards and reduces the risk of invented or foreign-law clauses.

Drafting principles AI should follow — and you should check

  • Precision: defined terms used consistently; obligations clear ("shall" or "must" for obligations, "may" for discretions).
  • Completeness: the document addresses the events that matter — termination, breach, disputes, notices, governing law and jurisdiction.
  • Coherence: no conflicting clauses or broken cross-references after edits.
  • Plain language where possible, especially for consumer and employment documents.
  • Jurisdictional fit: governing law, mandatory local rules (e.g., OHADA provisions, local consumer or labour protections) and enforceability.

Litigation drafting

Pleadings, submissions and correspondence carry the highest risk because they go to courts and opponents. Use AI for outlines, organising facts chronologically, drafting non-authoritative sections and checking consistency between facts and exhibits. Every authority, factual assertion and quotation must be verified. Some courts now require disclosure or certification regarding AI use in filings; check the rules and practice directions of the relevant court.

Client communication

AI is excellent at converting complex advice into clear explanations for clients — summaries, options with pros and cons, next steps. Ensure simplification does not change the legal meaning, and that the advice remains the lawyer's.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal research and drafting assistant. Step 1: help me frame a research question by jurisdiction, governing law, facts and sub-issues, with search terms in English and French. Step 2: when I paste authoritative extracts, help me structure an IRAC or syllogisme juridique analysis and identify weak points and counter-arguments. Step 3: adapt my approved template to the facts I give, flagging deviations and broken cross-references. Never invent authorities or quotations — mark any needed authority as [VERIFY].

📚 Glossary

  • IRAC / CREAC: structures for legal analysis and persuasive writing
  • Syllogisme juridique: civil-law reasoning from rule (major premise) to facts (minor premise) to conclusion
  • Pinpoint citation: reference to the exact page or paragraph
  • Precedent (drafting): an approved template document
  • Clause library: collection of approved standard clauses

📖 References

  • OHADA — Uniform Acts (official texts, ohada.org).
  • Garner, B. Legal Writing in Plain English.
  • Court practice directions on AI use — check the relevant jurisdiction.
  • Juricaf and AfricanLII — case-law databases (verify coverage).

quiz.q: A Cameroonian lawyer gets a land dispute from the North-West region. Following the five-step workflow, what should she do before asking AI to find authorities?
opts: Search the official gazette for any recent land statute amendments
Frame the question: jurisdiction, governing law, facts, posture and issues
Draft an IRAC outline so the AI knows which conclusion to support
Ask AI to list leading cases in English so she can read the key judgments
quiz.x: Step 1 is framing the question by jurisdiction, governing law, facts and procedural posture. Searching the gazette is step 2; asking AI for cases first risks fabricated authorities.

quiz.q: An AI tool provides a summary of a CCJA judgment that includes a sentence in quotation marks. The associate wants to include it in a memo. What is the correct approach?
opts: Paraphrase it instead, so there is no need to check the judgment itself
Use it with a footnote explaining that the quotation was generated by an AI research tool
Quote it only after copying it from the judgment and checking the reference
Use it, since the AI read the judgment and quoted it accurately
quiz.x: AI tools often quote language that is not in the source; text goes in quotation marks only when copied from the authoritative source with a checked reference. Paraphrasing still needs the source read.

quiz.q: A Paris-trained lawyer in Douala structures her analysis as major premise, minor premise, conclusion. A colleague trained in Buea prefers IRAC. Which statement is correct?
opts: The syllogism suits civil-law courts and IRAC is unsuitable there
Both are valid structures serving the same purpose of clear reasoning
CREAC should be used, as it is the international standard for memos
IRAC should be used, because courts in OHADA states expect it
quiz.x: The syllogisme juridique and IRAC serve the same purpose in different traditions; CREAC is used for persuasive writing. The choice depends on audience and tradition, not a single standard.

quiz.q: A firm's associate asks AI to draft a distribution agreement from scratch for a client in Libreville. Which workflow does the module prefer?
opts: Providing the firm's approved precedent and deal terms and asking for adaptation
Generating several drafts and selecting the one with the fewest legal errors
Asking AI to adapt a US distribution agreement the associate found online
Generating a draft from scratch and then comparing it clause by clause with the firm template
quiz.x: Reliable drafting begins from approved precedents rather than AI generating documents from nothing; this reduces invented or foreign-law clauses. Comparing a from-scratch draft is the runner-up but wastes time and imports errors.

quiz.q: A contract drafted with AI help uses 'the Supplier may deliver within 30 days' where the client needs a firm obligation. Which drafting principle is at issue?
opts: Completeness
Plain language
Coherence
Precision
quiz.x: Precision includes using 'shall' or 'must' for obligations and 'may' for discretion. Coherence concerns conflicting clauses and cross-references.

quiz.q: After several rounds of AI edits, a lease refers to 'clause 14.3' which no longer exists. Which principle requires a final check for this?
opts: Jurisdictional fit
Precision
Coherence
Completeness
quiz.x: Coherence requires no conflicting clauses or broken cross-references after edits. Completeness concerns whether the document addresses the events that matter.

quiz.q: A Texas litigator plans to file a motion drafted with AI help in a federal court. What should she check besides verifying every authority?
opts: Whether the opposing party also used AI, as that affects the burden
Whether the court's rules or standing orders require AI disclosure
Whether the judge has previously sanctioned lawyers for AI errors
Whether the AI tool's terms permit its outputs in court proceedings
quiz.x: Some courts require disclosure or certification of AI use; check the rules and practice directions for the relevant court. A judge's history is interesting but does not set obligations.

quiz.q: A lawyer asks AI to turn a 12-page advice letter on a tax dispute into a one-page client summary. What is the main risk to manage?
opts: The summary may disclose privileged advice to the client's own staff
The AI may refuse to summarise tax advice without a disclaimer
The client may treat the summary as a substitute for the full letter
Simplification may change the legal meaning of the advice given
quiz.x: AI excels at plain-language summaries, but simplification must not change the legal meaning, and the advice must remain the lawyer's. Clients relying on the summary is a related but secondary concern.

quiz.q: A junior asks AI to check a memo's IRAC structure. Which request makes best use of AI here?
opts: Ask AI which element is weak and which counter-arguments are missing
Ask AI to rewrite the memo in CREAC format for persuasiveness
Ask AI to add supporting authorities wherever the rule section looks thin
Ask AI to confirm that the conclusion is correct on the law
quiz.x: AI is helpful for testing structure: identifying weak elements, unaddressed counter-arguments and missing facts. Asking it to add authorities invites fabrication.

quiz.q: A Kenyan employment contract template adapted by AI omits mandatory local termination protections. Which drafting principle has failed?
opts: Precision of terms
Coherence of clauses
Jurisdictional fit
Plain language
quiz.x: Jurisdictional fit includes mandatory local rules such as labour protections and enforceability. Completeness is a runner-up, but the specific failure is ignoring local law.

facts.t: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion: the common structure for legal analysis.
facts.more: For persuasive writing, CREAC (Conclusion, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion) leads with the answer. AI is useful for testing which element is weak.

facts.t: The civil-law syllogisme juridique: major premise (rule), minor premise (facts), conclusion.
facts.more: In Cameroon's civil-law jurisdictions and OHADA practice it plays the role IRAC plays in common-law writing. Ask the AI to use the structure your forum expects.

facts.t: The module's AI-assisted research workflow, ending in verification.
facts.more: Frame, find in authoritative sources, read the texts, synthesise, then verify every citation, quotation, pinpoint and current status.

facts.t: AI tools often produce 'quotations' that don't appear in the source.
facts.more: Only put text in quotation marks if you copied it yourself from the authoritative source and checked the page or paragraph.

modules.t: Tool Study: The Legal AI Market
modules.d: Evaluating legal AI by accuracy, grounding, confidentiality and jurisdictional coverage.
modules.body:
A rapidly evolving market

Legal technology now includes general AI assistants, AI features inside established research databases, contract analysis platforms, e-discovery systems and practice-management tools. Products and features change quickly; evaluate by criteria and verify current capabilities, coverage and terms directly with providers.

Main categories

  • General AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot): drafting, summarising, translation, analysis of documents you provide. Not legal research databases; may fabricate authorities if asked for law without sources.
  • AI-enabled legal research platforms from established publishers (for example Thomson Reuters' Westlaw and CoCounsel, LexisNexis' Lexis+ AI): answers grounded in their databases with links to sources. Coverage of African, OHADA and Cameroonian law may be limited — check.
  • Free and regional legal information sources: OHADA official texts, Juricaf (francophone supreme court case law), AfricanLII and national legal information institutes, official gazettes. AI tools may not index these; lawyers must search them directly.
  • Contract analysis and lifecycle management: extracting clauses, comparing against playbooks, tracking obligations and renewals.
  • E-discovery and document review: technology-assisted review (TAR) and AI classification for large document sets, with statistical validation.
  • Practice management: time recording, billing, matter management and knowledge management with AI features.
Grounding is the key technical question. A tool that retrieves relevant documents from a trusted database and generates answers linked to those documents (often called retrieval-augmented generation) is generally more reliable than one answering from its training alone. But grounding can still fail — wrong document retrieved, misread holding, outdated law. Links make verification faster; they do not replace it.

Evaluation criteria

  1. Accuracy: test with real questions from your practice where you know the correct answer.
  2. Grounding and citations: does every answer link to sources you can open and check?
  3. Jurisdictional coverage: does it include your jurisdictions, languages, OHADA texts and recent decisions?
  4. Confidentiality and security: is client data used for training, where is it stored, what certifications and contractual protections exist, can you control retention?
  5. Privilege protection: do terms and architecture preserve confidentiality sufficient to avoid privilege concerns?
  6. Integration: with document management, email and practice systems.
  7. Auditability: are queries and outputs logged for supervision?
  8. Cost and value: licence cost relative to time saved and quality gained.

Testing a legal AI tool properly

Build a test set of 20–30 questions from your practice with known answers, including tricky ones: recently changed law, jurisdiction-specific questions, questions where the law is unsettled, and questions mixing OHADA and national law. Score each tool on correctness, citation accuracy, honesty about uncertainty and usefulness. A tool that admits uncertainty is safer than one that answers everything confidently.

Firm and department strategy

Many practices start with an approved general assistant under a business agreement for drafting and summarising client-provided documents, plus their existing research databases for authorities. Specialised platforms follow where volume and coverage justify them. Establish an approved tools list and prohibit unapproved tools for client work.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal technology evaluator. Help me build a test set of 25 questions from my practice area and jurisdictions, including recently changed law, OHADA versus national law questions, and unsettled issues. Then design a scoring rubric covering correctness, citation accuracy, honesty about uncertainty and usefulness, and a list of confidentiality and privilege questions to ask each vendor.

📚 Glossary

  • Grounding: basing AI answers on retrieved source documents
  • Retrieval-augmented generation: AI that retrieves relevant documents before generating an answer
  • TAR: technology-assisted review in document-heavy matters
  • Juricaf: database of francophone supreme court case law
  • Approved tools list: the tools permitted for client work

📖 References

  • Magesh, V. et al. (2024). Reliability of AI legal research tools. Stanford RegLab/HAI.
  • Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe (S.D.N.Y. 2012) — early judicial approval of TAR.
  • OHADA (ohada.org), Juricaf, AfricanLII — legal information sources.
  • Vendor documentation — verify current coverage and terms.

Whether it integrates with the firm's billing and time-recording software
Whether other firms in Douala have already adopted the same platform
Whether its price is lower than a general AI assistant for each user

quiz.q: A firm builds a 25-question test set to compare legal AI tools. Which design follows the module most closely?

Questions the partners find hardest, scored by the length of each answer

Generic legal questions from law school exams, for comparability with others

quiz.q: Two tools score similarly on correctness. Tool A sometimes says 'I am not certain; check the CCJA case law'. Tool B always gives a confident answer. Which is generally safer?

Tool A, because admitting uncertainty reduces the risk of reliance
Neither, since correctness scores are the main criterion that matters
Tool B, because uncertainty statements tend to signal weak grounding
quiz.x: A tool that admits uncertainty is safer than one that answers everything confidently. Honesty about uncertainty is one of the scoring criteria alongside correctness.

It removes the need to verify authorities, since answers are grounded
It ensures the law cited is current, as databases update in real time
It means the tool will refuse any question it cannot answer from sources
quiz.x: RAG retrieves documents before answering and is generally more reliable, but grounding can fail through wrong retrieval, misread holdings or outdated law. Links make verification faster, not unnecessary.

quiz.q: A US litigation team must review 400,000 emails for a dispute. Which approach does the module describe?
opts: Ask a general AI assistant to read the emails and list the relevant ones
Use technology-assisted review with statistical validation of results
Have junior lawyers review a random 1% sample and extrapolate to the rest
Use keyword searches instead, as courts have not accepted AI review
quiz.x: TAR and AI classification with statistical validation are standard for large reviews; courts have accepted TAR since Da Silva Moore (2012). Sampling alone is part of validation, not a review method.

quiz.q: A chambers in Accra is choosing a general AI assistant for drafting. Which contract term is most important for confidentiality?

A warranty that outputs will be legally accurate in Ghana
No training on inputs, controlled retention, confidentiality
A discount for multi-year licences and extra users

quiz.q: A legal department adopts a new AI tool. Its general counsel wants to check that juniors use it properly. Which evaluation criterion addresses this?

Cost and value: licence cost relative to time saved

quiz.q: A mid-size firm in Kampala is starting with AI. Which strategy reflects the module's description of common practice?
opts: Start with an approved general assistant plus existing research databases
Wait until AI tools are certified by the national law society
Let each lawyer choose their preferred consumer AI tool for drafting client work
Buy a specialised platform for every practice area at the same time
quiz.x: Many practices start with an approved general assistant under a business agreement plus existing databases; specialised platforms follow where justified. Unapproved consumer tools are prohibited for client work.

Accuracy, including currency of the law
Auditability of queries and outputs
Cost relative to time saved
quiz.x: Accuracy includes correct and current law; grounding can fail through outdated law. Auditability helps detect the error but is not what failed.

modules.d: Contract review playbooks, obligation tracking and regulatory compliance mapping with AI.
modules.body:
Contracts are data

Organisations hold thousands of contracts containing obligations, rights, deadlines and risks. Most are never systematically reviewed after signature — until something goes wrong. AI makes it practical to extract, compare and monitor contract terms at scale, turning static documents into manageable data.

The contract lifecycle

Request and drafting → negotiation and review → approval and signature → obligation management → renewal, amendment or termination. AI can assist at each stage: drafting from templates, comparing counterparty drafts against standards, summarising changes for approvers, extracting key dates and obligations into a register, and alerting before renewals and deadlines.

The review playbook

A contract review playbook records the organisation's positions on key clauses: preferred position, acceptable fallbacks, and unacceptable terms requiring escalation. Typical clauses: limitation of liability, indemnities, warranties, payment terms, intellectual property, confidentiality, data protection, termination, governing law and dispute resolution, and force majeure. With a playbook, AI can compare a counterparty draft clause by clause, classify each as standard, acceptable fallback or escalation, and propose redlines. Without a playbook, AI applies generic assumptions that may not reflect your risk appetite or your law.

Example. Playbook: "Limitation of liability — preferred: capped at 12 months' fees; fallback: capped at 2× annual fees; escalate: uncapped liability or exclusion of liability for our own data breaches." AI review: "Clause 11 caps supplier liability at fees paid in the previous 3 months — below fallback; propose 12 months and flag for negotiation." The lawyer confirms the reading and decides strategy.

Due diligence

In mergers, acquisitions and financings, AI can review large data rooms to identify change-of-control clauses, assignment restrictions, exclusivity, unusual indemnities and termination rights. Validate with sampling: lawyers review a statistically meaningful sample and all high-risk flags; the cost of a missed change-of-control clause can be severe.

Obligation management

Extracting obligations — delivery deadlines, reporting duties, service levels, notice periods, renewal dates — into a register with owners and alerts prevents missed deadlines, automatic renewals of unwanted contracts and breaches. AI extraction should be checked for key contracts; even small extraction errors on dates can have significant consequences.

Regulatory compliance mapping

Compliance teams must translate laws and regulations into internal obligations, controls and evidence. AI can help: summarising new regulations, mapping requirements to existing policies and controls, identifying gaps, and drafting control descriptions. For example, mapping data protection obligations — lawful basis, notices, data subject rights, security, breach notification, cross-border transfers — to the organisation's processes. As always, the authoritative regulatory text governs, and interpretation of ambiguous provisions requires legal judgement.

OHADA and cross-border contracts

Many contracts in Central and West Africa involve OHADA law, other national laws and international parties. Key considerations include choice of governing law, enforceability of arbitration clauses (OHADA Uniform Act on Arbitration; CCJA arbitration), language versions and which prevails, mandatory local rules, and currency and payment provisions. AI can help identify and compare these clauses across a portfolio; lawyers must assess enforceability.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my contract review assistant. First, help me build a review playbook for one contract type with preferred, fallback and escalation positions for the ten key clauses in this module, adapted to my governing law. Then, when I paste a counterparty draft (anonymised), compare it clause by clause, classify each as standard, fallback or escalation, propose redlines, and extract all dates and obligations into a register table. Mark any point needing lawyer judgement.

📚 Glossary

  • Review playbook: organisation's preferred, fallback and escalation positions on clauses
  • Change of control: clause triggered when ownership of a party changes
  • Obligation register: tracked list of contractual duties, deadlines and owners
  • Compliance mapping: linking legal requirements to internal controls and evidence
  • CCJA arbitration: arbitration administered under the OHADA Common Court of Justice and Arbitration

📖 References

  • World Commerce & Contracting — contract management resources.
  • OHADA — Uniform Act on Arbitration; CCJA Arbitration Rules.
  • OHADA — Uniform Act on General Commercial Law.
  • ICC — model contracts and arbitration rules.

quiz.q: A playbook says: limitation of liability preferred at 12 months' fees, fallback 2x annual fees, escalate if uncapped. A supplier draft caps liability at 6 months' fees. How should AI classify it?
opts: Standard, because a cap exists in the clause
Escalation, because it is less than 12 months
Acceptable, as it is within the 2x fallback
Below fallback; propose 12 months and flag it
quiz.x: A 6-month cap is below the preferred 12 months and outside the fallback, so propose 12 months and flag for negotiation, mirroring the module example. Escalation is for uncapped liability or excluded data-breach liability.

quiz.q: A supplier draft excludes all liability for data breaches caused by the supplier. Using the same playbook, what is the classification?
opts: Acceptable fallback, if the cap is otherwise 12 months
Standard, since data breach liability is often excluded
Escalation, as the playbook lists exclusion for data breaches
Fallback, as long as the supplier provides cyber insurance
quiz.x: The example playbook lists exclusion of liability for data breaches as requiring escalation. Insurance may mitigate risk but does not change the playbook classification.

quiz.q: A company's annual fees under a contract are 50 million FCFA. The playbook fallback is 2x annual fees. What is the fallback cap amount?
opts: 100 million FCFA
50 million FCFA
25 million FCFA
150 million FCFA
quiz.x: 2 x 50 million = 100 million FCFA. The preferred 12 months' fees would be 50 million.

quiz.q: An AI tool reviews 2,000 contracts in a data room for an acquisition in Nigeria. How should the lawyers validate the results?
opts: Ask a second AI tool to review the same contracts and compare results
Review a meaningful sample plus all high-risk flags like change of control
Review contracts above a value threshold manually and rely on the AI output for the rest
Trust the AI for low-risk clauses and review the high-risk ones yourself
quiz.x: Validate with a statistically meaningful sample and all high-risk flags; a missed change-of-control clause can be severe. Value thresholds can miss small contracts with critical clauses.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian company's contract renews automatically unless notice is given 90 days before 31 December. The AI register records the notice deadline as 1 October. What is the correct deadline?
opts: 1 November
30 September
2 October
1 October
quiz.x: Counting back 90 days from 31 December: 30 days to 1 December, 30 more to 1 November and 30 more to 2 October. The AI's 1 October is a day early, harmless here, but the same error the other way would miss the deadline; key dates must be checked.

quiz.q: A compliance team uses AI to map a new data protection law to internal controls. A provision on cross-border transfers is ambiguous. What should happen?
opts: Accept the AI's interpretation, since it read the full regulatory text
Wait for the regulator to issue guidance before mapping anything
Adopt the most restrictive reading suggested by the AI tool, to stay safe with the regulator
A lawyer interprets it from the authoritative text using legal judgement
quiz.x: The authoritative regulatory text governs, and interpretation of ambiguous provisions requires legal judgement. The most restrictive reading may be unnecessary and costly.

quiz.q: A contract between a Cameroonian buyer and a French seller has English and French versions. What should AI-assisted review specifically flag?
opts: Whether the English version uses British spelling
Whether both versions have the same page count
Which language version prevails if they differ
Whether the French version was drafted first
quiz.x: Language versions and which prevails are key considerations in cross-border contracts. The drafting order does not determine precedence.

quiz.q: A Yaounde in-house team asks an AI tool to review a 40-page supplier draft, but the company has never written a contract review playbook. What is the main limitation?
opts: It applies generic assumptions that may not reflect your risk or law
It cannot identify clauses in contracts written in French
It will refuse to propose redlines without explicit instructions
It works more slowly because it has no reference for comparison
quiz.x: Without a playbook, AI applies generic assumptions that may not reflect your risk appetite or law. Language capability is not the limitation described.

quiz.q: A dispute clause specifies CCJA arbitration under OHADA's Uniform Act on Arbitration. What must lawyers assess that AI cannot reliably decide?
opts: Whether the clause is in both language versions
Enforceability of the clause in the relevant jurisdictions
Whether the clause uses consistent defined terms
Whether the clause appears in the right section of the contract
quiz.x: AI can identify and compare clauses across a portfolio; lawyers assess enforceability. Defined terms and language consistency are checks AI can assist with.

quiz.q: A company has 1,500 contracts with renewal dates. Which AI use best prevents missed deadlines?
opts: Translating all contracts into one language for easier review
Classifying each contract by risk level using a general model
Summarising each contract into one paragraph for the legal team
Extracting obligations into a register with owners and alerts
quiz.x: Obligation registers with owners and alerts prevent missed deadlines and unwanted renewals. Summaries do not assign owners or trigger alerts.

facts.t: Contract lifecycle: draft, negotiate, sign, manage obligations, renew/amend/terminate.
facts.more: Most contracts are never reviewed after signature until something goes wrong. AI extraction turns them into data you can monitor.

facts.more: Without a playbook, AI applies generic assumptions that may not match your risk appetite or governing law.

facts.t: OHADA's court in Abidjan also administers its own arbitration system.

modules.d: Protecting client confidences, privilege and professional integrity when using AI.
modules.body:
Confidentiality is the first question

Lawyers owe clients duties of confidentiality that are among the strongest in professional life. Entering client information into an AI tool is a disclosure to a third party's system. Whether that is acceptable depends on the tool's terms, security and data use, the sensitivity of the information, applicable professional rules and, where needed, the client's informed consent.

Key questions before using any AI tool with client information: Does the provider use inputs to train models? Who at the provider can access data, and where is it stored? How long is it retained, and can you delete it? Is there a contract with confidentiality and data protection obligations? Does it meet security standards? ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024), for example, advises that lawyers must evaluate these risks and, for some tools — especially those that may disclose information to others or learn from it — obtain clients' informed consent before inputting confidential information. Your own jurisdiction's rules should be checked.

Practical rule for practices. Client-confidential and privileged information goes only into approved tools under business or enterprise agreements with appropriate confidentiality, security and no-training terms. Consumer versions of AI tools, personal accounts and unapproved apps are prohibited for client work. When in doubt, anonymise or do not use the tool.

Legal privilege

Legal professional privilege (or the attorney–client privilege and work-product protection in some systems, or secret professionnel in civil-law traditions) protects certain communications and materials from disclosure. Privilege can be lost through disclosure to third parties outside the protected relationship. Whether using an AI provider waives privilege depends on jurisdiction, the tool's confidentiality arrangements and how it is used. Reduce risk by using tools under strict confidentiality terms, limiting what is shared, and following firm policy.

Supervision and responsibility

Partners and supervising lawyers remain responsible for work produced by juniors, paralegals and non-lawyer staff, including their use of AI. Practices should establish policies, training, approved tools and review procedures. "The AI did it" is not a defence in disciplinary proceedings or before a court.

Fees and billing

If AI reduces the time taken, hourly billing must reflect time actually spent. Charging clients for hours saved by AI, or for the lawyer's time learning a general tool, is generally inappropriate. Practices may consider value-based or fixed fees that reflect the value delivered. Costs of AI tools may be charged only where permitted and agreed. Transparency with clients about billing arrangements protects trust.

Candour, fairness and the court

Lawyers must not mislead courts on law or fact, must correct errors promptly, and must comply with any court rules on AI disclosure. They must also deal fairly with opponents — for example, not using AI to fabricate evidence or alter documents. Deepfake audio, video and images present new evidentiary challenges; lawyers should be alert to the possibility that evidence has been manipulated and seek authentication where appropriate.

Communication with clients

Clients should be informed about significant uses of AI that affect their matter, especially where confidential information is involved, where it affects fees, or where clients have expressed preferences. Many corporate clients now issue outside-counsel guidelines specifying AI use requirements; follow them.

Bias and access to justice

AI can widen access to legal information for people who cannot afford lawyers — but it can also provide confident wrong advice to those least able to detect it, and reproduce biases in legal data. Lawyers and legal organisations deploying public-facing legal AI should design for accuracy, clear limitations, escalation to human help and fairness.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal ethics advisor. I will describe how I plan to use an AI tool on a client matter. Analyse the confidentiality, privilege, supervision, fee and candour implications, list the questions I must answer about the tool's terms, state whether client informed consent may be needed, and draft a short client communication explaining our AI use. Remind me to verify the rules of my own bar or law society.

📚 Glossary

  • Legal professional privilege: protection of certain lawyer–client communications from disclosure
  • Secret professionnel: civil-law professional secrecy obligation
  • Informed consent: client agreement after explanation of risks and alternatives
  • Outside-counsel guidelines: client rules for external lawyers, increasingly including AI
  • Deepfake: AI-manipulated audio, video or image

📖 References

  • American Bar Association — Formal Opinion 512 (2024), Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools.
  • Law Society of England and Wales — Generative AI: the essentials.
  • Bar associations and law societies — check your jurisdiction's AI guidance.
  • Barreau du Cameroun — rules of professional conduct (verify current texts).

quiz.q: A Douala associate wants to paste a client's draft share purchase agreement into a free consumer AI app. The firm has an enterprise tool with no-training terms. What should she do?
opts: Ask the client's in-house team whether they mind before using the app
Use the consumer app after removing the client's name from the document
Use the approved enterprise tool, or anonymise if unsure, per firm policy
Use the consumer app with chat history turned off to limit retention
quiz.x: Client-confidential information goes into approved tools under business agreements; consumer versions are prohibited for client work. Removing a name often fails to anonymise deal terms.

quiz.q: ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024) is discussed in a US firm's ethics training. What does it advise about some AI tools?
opts: Lawyers must disclose all AI use to opposing counsel in litigation matters
Client informed consent may be needed before inputting confidential information
Consent may be skipped for any tool if the lawyer reviews outputs before use
Just bar-approved AI tools may be used for client work in each US state
quiz.x: Opinion 512 advises evaluating risks and, for some tools especially those that may disclose or learn from information, obtaining informed consent. Rules differ by state, so check your jurisdiction.

quiz.q: A firm uses an AI provider for privileged strategy memos. A partner asks whether privilege is waived. What is the best answer?
opts: Privilege is preserved if the provider is based in the same country
Privilege is preserved as long as every memo is clearly marked 'privileged and confidential'
Privilege is waived whenever any third party processes the material
It depends on jurisdiction, confidentiality terms and how the tool is used
quiz.x: Whether using an AI provider waives privilege depends on jurisdiction, the tool's confidentiality arrangements and use. Reduce risk with strict confidentiality terms and limited sharing.

quiz.q: A paralegal used AI to draft a letter with an error that reached a client. The supervising partner says 'the AI did it'. What is the correct view?
opts: The supervising lawyer remains responsible for the work produced
No one is responsible if the firm's AI policy was followed
The AI provider is responsible under its terms of service
The paralegal is responsible because they operated the tool
quiz.x: Supervising lawyers remain responsible for work by juniors and staff, including AI use; 'the AI did it' is not a defence.

quiz.q: A task that previously took 5 hours now takes 1.5 hours with AI. The lawyer bills hourly at 100,000 FCFA. What is the appropriate charge for that task?
opts: 350,000 FCFA, splitting the time saved evenly
250,000 FCFA, adding time spent learning the tool
150,000 FCFA, reflecting time actually spent
500,000 FCFA, reflecting the value of the work
quiz.x: Hourly billing must reflect time actually spent: 1.5 x 100,000 = 150,000 FCFA. Value-based fees are possible only if agreed in advance; billing for learning a general tool is generally inappropriate.

quiz.q: During litigation in Lagos, a party submits a recording of the other side's director making admissions. The director denies it. What should the lawyer consider?
opts: The recording may be a deepfake; seek authentication where appropriate
Accept it, since recordings are generally reliable evidence
Object automatically, since AI tools could have created any recording in the case
Ask the court to exclude all recordings in the proceedings
quiz.x: Deepfakes present new evidentiary challenges; lawyers should be alert to manipulation and seek authentication where appropriate. Objecting automatically lacks basis.

quiz.q: A corporate client's outside-counsel guidelines require approval before using AI on its matters. A firm partner has not read them. What should the firm do?
opts: Follow its own AI policy, which takes priority over client guidelines
Use AI for internal tasks alone, as these are not covered by guidelines
Ask the client to remove the AI clause from the guidelines
Follow the client's guidelines on AI use for that client's matters
quiz.x: Many corporate clients now issue outside-counsel guidelines specifying AI requirements; follow them. Firm policy does not override client instructions.

quiz.q: A legal aid NGO wants to deploy a public chatbot giving tenancy advice in Nairobi. What design priority does the module stress?
opts: Making the chatbot available in English to reach the most users
Accuracy, clear limits, escalation to human help and fairness
Minimising costs so the service can reach more people quickly
Making the answers as detailed as possible on every question
quiz.x: Public-facing legal AI should be designed for accuracy, clear limitations, escalation to human help and fairness. Detailed answers risk confident wrong advice.

quiz.q: A US firm wants to charge clients a fee for its AI tool licence. What is the best guidance?
opts: It may charge the cost to the clients whose matters used the tool most often
It may add the cost to any client invoice as a disbursement
It may not charge for AI, as it is part of normal office overhead
It may charge tool costs only where permitted and agreed with the client
quiz.x: Costs of AI tools may be charged only where permitted and agreed. Charging without agreement breaches transparency, and rules vary by jurisdiction.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian civil-law notary works under secret professionnel. A colleague says this is identical to US attorney-client privilege. What is the best response?
opts: US privilege is broader, so it should be applied in Cameroon
They are identical across systems, so the same rules apply
They are related protections but differ by legal tradition and rules
Secret professionnel applies to notaries but not to practising lawyers
quiz.x: Privilege and secret professionnel serve similar purposes but differ across systems; check jurisdiction-specific rules.

facts.t: ABA Op. 512: some AI tools may need the client's informed consent before confidential data goes in.
facts.more: Especially tools that may disclose information to others or learn from it. Other jurisdictions differ, so check your own bar or law society.

facts.t: Privilege can be lost by disclosure outside the protected relationship.
facts.more: Whether using an AI provider waives privilege depends on the jurisdiction, confidentiality terms and how the tool is used. Strict terms and limited sharing reduce the risk.

facts.t: Civil-law systems protect client confidences as 'secret professionnel'.
facts.more: In Cameroon's civil-law tradition and other francophone jurisdictions, it does the work of privilege and confidentiality. Check the Barreau du Cameroun rules for current texts.

facts.t: Hourly billing must reflect time actually spent, even when AI saved hours.
facts.more: Billing for hours AI saved, or for learning a general tool, is generally inappropriate. Fixed or value-based fees can share the gains fairly.

All authorities will be verified by a lawyer before filing.

If the opponent's audio exhibit seems altered, we will seek authentication.

Lawyers stay responsible. 'The AI did it' is not a defence.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the managing partner's AI week
plaibox.intro: You are managing partner of a 12-lawyer firm in Douala. Scoring: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: A senior associate pasted a privileged board memo into a consumer chatbot.
o: Assess what was shared, contain it, and weigh notifying the client
Incident response first: scope, containment and an honest assessment of notification duties.
Tell her privately not to do it again, and simply move on
Corrective, but it ignores possible confidentiality and privilege consequences.
Delete the chat history and say nothing to anyone
Concealment compounds the breach and may violate duties to the client.

steps.s: A bank client's guidelines now require prior approval for any AI use.
o: Comply, but only on new matters from next quarter
Partial. The guidelines likely apply now to all matters.
Map current AI use on their matters and request approval
Following client guidelines and communicating openly protects the relationship.
Ignore it: our tool is enterprise-grade and secure
Contract and trust both require compliance regardless of tool quality.

steps.s: AI lets the firm draft standard leases in 1 hour instead of 4.
o: Keep billing 4 hours: the client gets the same document
Billing time not spent is unreasonable.
Offer a fixed fee that reflects value and shares the savings
A transparent, value-based fee fits the efficiency gain.
Bill 1 hour plus a charge for the AI licence
Possible only if permitted and agreed in advance. Check first.

Deepfakes are a real evidentiary risk. Authentication is the proper step.
Publicly accuse the opposing party of fabricating it

Accept it, but argue it was taken out of context

plaibox.win: Sound leadership: contain incidents, follow client guidelines, bill fairly, and test evidence.
plaibox.lose: Revisit confidentiality, fees and candour. Lawyers stay responsible for the tools and the people they supervise.

modules.d: A written protocol governing responsible AI use in your practice or legal department.
modules.body:
From individual use to practice-wide protocol

Your capstone is a practical AI protocol for your firm, chambers, legal department or compliance team. It should allow lawyers to use AI confidently for the right tasks while protecting clients, courts and the practice.

Protocol components

  1. Purpose and scope: which people, matters and tools the protocol covers.
  2. Principles: lawyer responsibility, confidentiality, verification, candour, fairness and client trust.
  3. Approved tools and uses: a list of approved tools with permitted uses (for example summarising client-provided documents, drafting from precedents, translation with review) and prohibited uses (for example relying on AI for authorities without verification, entering client data into unapproved tools).
  4. Data and confidentiality rules: classification of information, anonymisation requirements, client consent triggers, and client guideline compliance.
  5. Verification standard: every authority, quotation, pinpoint, statutory reference and factual assertion verified in authoritative sources before use; currency checks.
  6. Court and regulatory rules: compliance with practice directions on AI disclosure and certification.
  7. Supervision: review requirements by seniority and matter risk; training for juniors and staff.
  8. Billing: rules on time recording and fee arrangements involving AI.
  9. Incident response: what to do if an error is discovered or confidential data is exposed — including prompt correction with courts and notification obligations.
  10. Review: owner and review date.
Make verification visible. Many practices add a simple verification checklist to the file for any AI-assisted court filing or opinion: authorities retrieved and read; quotations checked; pinpoints confirmed; currency checked; facts traced to evidence; reviewer name and date. It takes minutes and could prevent sanctions.

Implementation

Approve the protocol through practice leadership; procure approved tools; train every lawyer and staff member, including practical exercises showing how AI fabricates authorities; integrate checklists into document management; and review after three months. Measure time saved, error and near-miss reports, client feedback and compliance.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit the protocol (no more than six pages plus checklists), one completed verification checklist for a sample AI-assisted document, and a one-page briefing for practice leadership. Your mentor reviews it for completeness, legal accuracy for your jurisdiction and practicality.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal AI protocol drafter. Using my practice type, jurisdictions and approved tools, draft a protocol with the ten components from this module in under six pages. Include a one-page verification checklist for AI-assisted filings and opinions, and an incident response procedure for errors and data exposure. Flag every rule I must confirm against my bar or law society and court practice directions.

Going deeper — capstone playbook: your Practice AI Protocol

A protocol earns trust when partners, associates and support staff can follow it on a deadline. Reviewers look for precise verification duties, confidentiality rules that fit your jurisdiction and client base, and evidence that the protocol was tested on a realistic matter. Court and bar guidance on AI is evolving; cite the current rules that apply to you and date your review.

Step-by-step timeline.

  • Week 1 — Survey and rules. Inventory current AI use in the practice; collect professional conduct rules, data protection law, client outside-counsel guidelines and any court practice directions on AI.
  • Week 2 — Draft. Write principles, approved/prohibited uses, the data classification table and the verification standard; draft the filing verification checklist.
  • Week 3 — Pilot. Apply the protocol to one past or hypothetical matter: a research memo or contract review done with AI, fully verified, with time and error log.
  • Week 4 — Finalise. Add supervision, billing and incident response; seek comment from a senior lawyer and IT or data protection lead; present.

Deliverables checklist.

  • ☐ Practice AI Protocol
  • ☐ Approved tools and uses table
  • ☐ Data classification and client consent triggers
  • ☐ Verification checklist for AI-assisted work product
  • ☐ Pilot report (task, time, errors found, lessons)
  • ☐ Incident response flowchart

Assessment rubric (weighted).

  • Professional duties and law — 25%: competence, confidentiality, candour and supervision correctly addressed
  • Verification standard — 20%: precise, auditable and realistic
  • Confidentiality and data — 20%: classification, tools and client consent clear
  • Pilot evidence — 15%: protocol tested with honest findings
  • Practicality and clarity — 20%: usable by staff at every level
Worked mini-example. A commercial law firm in Douala pilots the protocol on an OHADA-related contract review. An approved enterprise tool summarises an anonymised supply agreement and flags clauses against the firm's playbook; the associate verifies every flagged clause against the source and checks the cited Uniform Act provisions in official texts. The AI missed a governing-law conflict and suggested one article reference that did not exist; both are caught by the checklist. Review time falls, but the pilot report records the errors and adds a rule: no article citation is used unless retrieved from an authoritative source.

Common failure modes.

  • Banning AI completely, driving use underground.
  • A verification rule that says "check everything" without defining what and how.
  • Ignoring client guidelines that restrict AI use.
  • No incident procedure for a discovered fabricated citation.
  • Billing practices that charge for time AI saved without client transparency.

Submission and presentation structure.

  • 1. Why the practice needs a protocol (risks and opportunities)
  • 2. Principles and approved/prohibited uses
  • 3. Confidentiality and verification standards
  • 4. Pilot findings
  • 5. Supervision, billing, incidents and review
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a senior professional-responsibility reviewer. Here is my draft AI protocol [paste] and my jurisdiction [state it]. Identify gaps against duties of competence, confidentiality, supervision and candour to the court; list the authoritative sources I should check for current AI rules (do not state rules you are unsure of); and draft a one-page verification checklist for AI-assisted court filings that a junior associate could follow.

📚 Glossary

  • AI protocol: practice-wide rules for responsible AI use
  • Verification checklist: record of checks performed on AI-assisted work
  • Incident response: steps taken when an error or data exposure is discovered
  • Near miss: an error caught before it caused harm

📖 References

  • American Bar Association — Formal Opinion 512 (2024).
  • Law Society of England and Wales — Generative AI guidance.
  • Court practice directions on AI — check each relevant court.

quiz.q: A Douala firm's AI protocol lists approved tools but no prohibited uses. Which addition best fits the module?
opts: Prohibit relying on AI authorities without verification and unapproved tools
Add a section on the history of AI use in the legal profession
Add a statement encouraging lawyers to use AI wherever possible
Add a list of AI vendors the firm has evaluated but not yet approved
quiz.x: Approved tools and uses should include prohibited uses such as relying on AI for authorities without verification and entering client data into unapproved tools.

quiz.q: A firm's verification checklist for AI-assisted filings includes authorities retrieved and read, quotations checked and pinpoints confirmed. What item is most clearly missing?
opts: The name of the AI tool that produced the first draft of the filing
Currency checks, facts traced to evidence, reviewer name and date
The number of hours saved by AI use on the filing overall
Client approval of the AI tool used on the matter in advance
quiz.x: The checklist includes currency checks, facts traced to evidence and reviewer name and date. Tool names and hours saved are useful data but not verification steps.

quiz.q: A lawyer discovers a fabricated citation in a brief already filed in a Nairobi court. What should the protocol's incident response require?
opts: Wait to see if opposing counsel notices before taking any action
Replace the citation silently in the next filing to the court
Prompt correction with the court and any required notifications
Internal review first, with notice to the court just after the hearing
quiz.x: Incident response includes prompt correction with courts and notification obligations. Delaying until after the hearing compounds the breach of candour.

quiz.q: A 40-lawyer firm in Kinshasa has drafted its AI protocol and asks which implementation plan best reflects good practice.
opts: Pilot it with the partners first and roll it out to juniors after a full year
Approve it, procure tools, train everyone with exercises, review at three months
Publish it on the firm's website and client portal to build client confidence
Email the protocol to all staff and require a signed acknowledgement within a week
quiz.x: Implementation includes approval, procurement, training every lawyer and staff member with practical exercises, integrating checklists, and review after three months.

quiz.q: A protocol requires the same review for a routine NDA as for a Supreme Court brief. What should change?
opts: Let each lawyer decide the review level for their own work
Require partner review of every document regardless of type
Remove review for NDAs, since they are low-risk documents
Set review requirements by seniority and matter risk
quiz.x: Supervision should set review requirements by seniority and matter risk. Partner review of everything is impractical.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian firm's draft AI protocol says nothing about when a client must agree before its documents are processed by an AI tool. Which component should cover this?
opts: Data and confidentiality rules
Review owner and date
Purpose and scope
Billing and fee arrangements
quiz.x: Data and confidentiality rules include classification, anonymisation, client consent triggers and client guideline compliance.

quiz.q: After three months, a firm reviews its AI protocol. Which measures does the module suggest tracking?
opts: Number of AI tools purchased and their total licence costs
Volume of documents produced with AI in each department per month
Time saved, errors and near misses, client feedback, compliance
Number of lawyers who passed an external AI certification exam
quiz.x: Measure time saved, error and near-miss reports, client feedback and compliance. Volume alone does not measure quality or risk.

quiz.q: A capstone protocol submitted by a legal department in Abidjan runs 15 pages. What should the author do?
opts: Split it into separate protocols for each practice area
Keep it, as more detail makes the protocol more complete
Add an executive summary and keep the full 15 pages
Condense to six pages plus checklists for practicality
quiz.x: The capstone limits the protocol to six pages plus checklists. An executive summary helps but does not meet the requirement.

quiz.q: A protocol says court rules on AI disclosure are 'outside its scope'. Why is this a problem?
opts: Compliance with court practice directions on AI is a core component
Disclosure rules are set by bar associations, not by individual courts
Courts generally ban AI use in filings, so the protocol must state it
It means the firm cannot use AI for any litigation work in practice
quiz.x: Court and regulatory rules on AI disclosure and certification are a protocol component. Courts vary; some require disclosure, so check each relevant court.

quiz.q: A legal department in Kigali adopted an AI protocol last year, but the document names no owner and sets no review date. What risk does this create?
opts: The protocol may come into conflict with the firm's billing and time-recording policy
The protocol may become outdated as tools and rules change
The protocol may be too long for staff to read
The protocol may be rejected by the firm's insurer
quiz.x: The review component requires an owner and review date so the protocol stays current as tools and rules change.

facts.t: Components in the practice AI protocol.
facts.more: Scope, principles, approved tools and uses, data rules, verification standard, court rules, supervision, billing, incident response, and review.

facts.t: The verification checklist for every AI-assisted filing or opinion.
facts.more: Authorities retrieved and read, quotations checked, pinpoints confirmed, currency checked, facts traced to evidence, reviewer name and date. It takes minutes and could prevent sanctions.

facts.t: When to review the protocol after rollout.
facts.more: Measure time saved, error and near-miss reports, client feedback and compliance, then adjust.

facts.t: An error caught before it caused harm. Log it.
facts.more: Near-miss reports are the best early warning of where AI is misleading your lawyers. A no-blame culture gets them reported.
